rv.q: Mezzocchi has created something extraordinary—a memoir play of uncommon formal beauty and emotional magnitude, one that gazes directly into oblivion and answers it, stubbornly and magnificently, with love.

73 Seconds is his attempt, perhaps too little and perhaps too late, to make something out of that nothing. It's an apology, an elegy, and an artifact: you can see the consciousness that has gone into crafting this story by which his mother will be remembered.
After a while, his performance becomes plodding, and his replication of Rosemary’s Yankee-accented voice is not persuasive.
Still, 73 Seconds remains worth seeing for its immersive experience alone.
